newsitem.title: CANADA: Earth Summit pledges abandoned, says former head.
newsitem.headline: Earth Summit pledges abandoned, says former head.

text.p: The world's developed countries have not fulfilled pledges made at the 1992 Earth Summit to fund environmentally sustainable development, the former head of the summit said on Friday.

Maurice Strong, who was Secretary-General of the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development four years ago, told reporters that despite lofty promises made in Rio de Janeiro, the developed world was reneging on its commitments.

During a news conference after a panel discussion at the World Conservation Congress, a 10-day gathering of 2,000 environmental specialists, Strong said the global environment was still deteriorating.
"We have not made the fundamental change of course the Rio indicated was absolutely essential if we are going to have a sustainable future in the 21st century," Strong said.

In Rio, world governments pledged to save the planet's forests, prevent global warming and protect endangered species. They also agreed to a blueprint incorporating environmental considerations into economic development around the world.
But little real progress has been made, even though there was evidence that so-called environmentally sustainable development offered the most promising social and economic returns, he said.
Strong's comments were echoed by other members of the panel.
James Gustave Speth, administrator of the U.N. Development Programme, blamed developed countries for the "breach of trust" of the Rio commitments.

Despite increases in humanitarian aid to refugees and countries in crisis, the world's industrialised nations have not kept their Rio pledge to dramatically boost economic development assistance to developing countries.
"Instead, development cooperation (assistance) has declined by one-fourth, if you take out the humanitarian aid component," Speth said.
Yet the developing world had begun to realise that its environmental resource base, which is especially vital to the most impoverished nations, was rapidly deteriorating, he said.

He warned that by refusing to increase funding for development, industrialised nations risked paying a much higher price down the road for humanitarian assistance, disease control, access to minerals and resources, peacekeeping, and the containment of armed conflict.
